package_info.package_name: Multiple RED-LILI dependency confusion packages (e.g., cspell-version-pin, glints-sdk, kusto-language-service, lorawan-devices, etc.)
package_info.package_versions: 99.10.13 and others (varies per package, see CSV list)
package_info.why_malicious: These packages are part of a large-scale, fully-automated dependency confusion attack campaign. They impersonate legitimate @azure scoped packages, contain obfuscated malicious payloads, and exfiltrate data to attacker-controlled domains. The attacker uses automation to create unique npm accounts per package, making detection and takedown more difficult.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During installation (postinstall), the code checks for specific hostnames/usernames/paths to avoid execution in analysis environments, then collects environment variables and potentially other system data, and exfiltrates this data via HTTPS POST to attacker-controlled domains (rt11.ml, 33mail.ga).

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code executes automatically on install, performs anti-analysis checks, collects sensitive data, and exfiltrates it to an external server.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal npm packages should not exfiltrate environment variables or system data during installation, nor should they contain anti-analysis logic.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate packages may collect telemetry, but not at install-time, and not with anti-analysis or obfuscation.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During installation, the package.json 'preinstall' script triggers execution of the malicious index.js payload.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The use of a preinstall script to execute arbitrary code is a common vector for supply chain attacks.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages rarely use preinstall scripts, and when they do, it is for setup, not for running obfuscated or network-exfiltrating code.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some build tools use preinstall for setup, but not for data exfiltration.
key_indicators: Presence of 'preinstall' script pointing to index.js
No legitimate setup or build logic

execution_context.file_location: automation script (Python, not in package, but part of attack infrastructure)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At attack infrastructure runtime, the script automates creation of npm accounts, handles OTP email via attacker-controlled SMTP, and publishes malicious packages in bulk.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Automated creation of hundreds of npm accounts and packages is highly abnormal and designed to evade detection and takedown.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal package publication is manual or CI/CD-based, not mass-automated with disposable accounts.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: CI/CD automation for legitimate package publishing, but not at this scale or with disposable accounts.
key_indicators: Use of attacker-controlled email domains for OTP

attack_chain.action: Automated enumeration of target package names (e.g., @azure scope) and generation of similar names.
attack_chain.leads_to: Creation of malicious npm accounts and packages

attack_chain.action: Automated creation of unique npm user accounts using attacker-controlled email domains and handling OTP via Interactsh SMTP.
Automated publishing of malicious packages with obfuscated payloads and preinstall scripts.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious packages available on npm registry

attack_chain.action: Malicious package is installed by victim (dependency confusion).
Malicious payload (index.js) runs anti-analysis checks, collects environment/system data, and exfiltrates to attacker domain.

behavioral_signatures: npm package with preinstall/postinstall scripts executing index.js
Obfuscated JavaScript code in index.js that performs network requests
Anti-analysis logic checking for specific hostnames/usernames/paths
Bulk publishing of similarly-named packages from unique, disposable accounts
network_indicators: HTTPS requests to rt11.ml, 33mail.ga, or similar attacker-controlled domains
SMTP/DNS traffic to attacker infrastructure during npm account creation
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for npm packages with preinstall/postinstall scripts, especially those executing obfuscated JavaScript. Flag packages with randomized author/email fields or disposable domains. Detect network connections to known attacker domains (rt11.ml, 33mail.ga) during or after package installation. Monitor for bulk publishing activity from unique accounts. Use static analysis to identify anti-analysis logic and suspicious data exfiltration code in package payloads.
